EXECUTIVE MANAGEMENT OVERVIEW:
Nebius’s senior management team is assessed as HIGH QUALITY, with an overall management rating of 8/10. The team is a material positive factor in the investment case because Nebius is not being run as a generic GPU reseller or opportunistic AI-infrastructure financing vehicle; it is being led by a founder-operator with a long operating history in search, infrastructure, distributed systems, machine learning, data centers, and large-scale engineering organizations. The most important positive attributes are Arkady Volozh’s prior company-building record at Yandex, the concentration of technical leadership from the Yandex infrastructure and product ecosystem, the company’s ability to secure strategic validation from NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Meta, and the rapid conversion of that credibility into capital, contracted capacity, and revenue growth. The most important negatives are founder voting control, limited minority-shareholder influence, still-unremediated internal-control weaknesses, very high capital intensity, customer and supplier concentration, and execution risk around multi-GW power procurement, construction, GPU deployment, financing, and customer utilization. The resulting assessment is that management is an asset to the equity story, but not a full de-risking mechanism. Management quality supports a premium to weaker neocloud peers, but governance and control deficiencies argue against applying a clean hyperscaler-quality multiple. (Stock Titan)
The investment implication is that Nebius should be underwritten primarily as a management-execution compounder with unusually high upside/downside convexity. The positive case depends on management’s ability to transform technical credibility and strategic partnerships into economically attractive capacity at scale. Recent operating evidence is favorable: Q1 2026 group revenue was $399.0M, up 684% year over year, Nebius AI Cloud revenue was $389.7M, up 841%, AI Cloud represented 98% of group revenue, annualized run-rate revenue reached $1.92B, and AI Cloud adjusted EBITDA was $174.0M, implying a 45% margin. The management team also entered Q1 2026 with more than $9B of cash, had raised $6.3B of capital in the quarter, and disclosed more than 3.5 GW of contracted capacity, with a target of more than 4 GW by year-end 2026. Those data points strongly support the view that management has shifted Nebius from post-divestiture repositioning into a scaled AI infrastructure buildout. (SEC)
The key offset is that the same management model carries structural governance and financial-control risk. Arkady Volozh beneficially controls approximately 52% of the voting power, enabling Nebius to qualify as a Nasdaq “controlled company.” Although Nebius currently maintains a majority-independent board, an independent audit committee, and an independent compensation committee, the nomination and governance committee is not entirely independent and is chaired by Volozh. This structure materially reduces the practical probability of successful activism, board-driven CEO replacement, or minority-led governance intervention if execution deteriorates. The appropriate investment treatment is a founder-led premium for technical vision and speed, combined with a governance discount for voting control, dual-class economics, and limited external accountability. (Stock Titan)
The highest-probability positive investment outcome is that Nebius continues to convert power, capital, and GPU supply into contracted AI Cloud revenue faster than the market expects. The highest-severity negative outcome is not ordinary SaaS-style deceleration; it is a capital-intensive execution failure in which construction delays, GPU underutilization, customer concentration, financing cost, dilution, or control weaknesses reduce confidence in unit economics. Management’s quality therefore directly affects position sizing. A larger position is more defensible if active capacity, customer diversification, capex/MW, utilization, and internal-control remediation progress in parallel. A smaller or more tactical position is more appropriate if revenue growth remains driven by a limited set of hyperscale customers, capex reporting remains difficult to audit, or financing relies increasingly on dilution and structured obligations rather than self-funding cash generation.
CEO ASSESSMENT: ARKADY VOLOZH
Arkady Volozh is the central figure in the Nebius management assessment. His CEO rating is 8.5/10, reflecting unusually strong founder-market fit, deep technical credibility, and a differentiated record of building large-scale technology infrastructure, offset by concentrated control, key-person dependence, and residual geopolitical/reputational complexity. Volozh is the principal founder of Nebius, was appointed executive director and CEO in August 2024, and previously served as founder, executive director, and CEO of Yandex between 2000 and 2022. His earlier entrepreneurial record includes CompTek and InfiNet Wireless, and he has been involved with technology assets such as Face.com, Getir, and Neurosteer. His academic background in applied mathematics is directly relevant to a company whose competitive edge depends on distributed systems, AI infrastructure, optimization, and technically sophisticated capital allocation. (Stock Titan)
The Yandex record is highly relevant to the investment case. Volozh did not merely scale a consumer internet brand; he built an engineering-centric technology platform that required search infrastructure, data-center capacity, advertising systems, maps, cloud, machine-learning capabilities, and high-performing technical talent. Reuters has described Yandex as having launched with less than $100,000 of revenue, later becoming Russia’s dominant online-search company, listing on Nasdaq, and reaching a market capitalization of roughly . Official Yandex disclosures also showed strong pre-war operating momentum, including 2021 revenue growth of 54% on a like-for-like basis and a Q4 2021 Russian search share of 60.2%. This background matters because Nebius’s execution challenge is not purely financial; it requires the assembly of engineering talent, infrastructure procurement, custom software, customer credibility, and operational reliability at scale. (Reuters)
Volozh’s post-2022 restructuring record is also a positive, though not an uncomplicated one. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Volozh stepped down from Yandex after EU sanctions were imposed, later criticized the invasion, and was removed from the EU sanctions list in March 2024. Nebius was subsequently separated from Yandex’s Russian assets, with the sale of those assets completed under severe constraints, including a mandatory discount framework, and Nebius retained the non-Russian businesses that now form the basis of the AI infrastructure platform. This sequence demonstrates crisis-management capability, legal and financial complexity management, and willingness to reposition the company away from Russia-related assets. It also leaves a residual reputational diligence requirement, particularly for U.S. customers, U.S. capital providers, export-control counterparties, and government-adjacent enterprise customers. (Reuters)
The CEO’s strongest green flag is the combination of founder ownership, product intuition, technical depth, and demonstrated ability to attract elite engineers. Nebius’s own strategic materials emphasize more than 1,000 top-tier AI engineers, a full-stack AI cloud model, deep experience designing servers with ODMs, an NVIDIA relationship, ownership or control across key parts of the stack, and a claimed 20%-25% total-cost-of-ownership advantage versus less vertically integrated approaches. The current Q1 2026 evidence supports the strategic credibility of that model: management disclosed a 98% AI Cloud revenue mix, 45% AI Cloud adjusted EBITDA margin, rapidly expanding pipeline, new U.S. GW-scale data-center sites, and more than 75% owned capacity within its contracted power base. Those are not typical outcomes for a management team lacking customer access, supplier credibility, or infrastructure execution competence. (SEC)
The CEO’s most material red flag is governance concentration. Volozh’s approximately 52% voting control creates decisive strategic authority and protects long-duration infrastructure investment from short-term market pressure. That is useful in a business where financing, power procurement, and GPU deployment require multi-year conviction. However, the same control structure limits external accountability and makes minority-shareholder rights economically weaker than in a 1-share, 1-vote structure. The CEO can effectively determine board composition, strategic direction, M&A appetite, capital allocation, and tolerance for dilution or leverage. The founder-control premium should therefore be applied only if execution remains visibly superior. If operating milestones slip, the same control structure could become a material valuation overhang because governance-driven corrective mechanisms would be limited. (Stock Titan)
The CEO’s capital-allocation record since the Nebius relaunch is favorable but still early. Nebius entered the post-divestiture phase with significant cash and no debt, then moved quickly into a much larger capital program as demand and customer commitments expanded. By Q1 2026, the company had raised $6.3B of capital, including $4.3B of convertible notes, secured a $2B strategic investment from NVIDIA, disclosed a Meta agreement with up to $27B of 5-year potential value, and continued to reference long-term strategic customer commitments including Microsoft and Meta. The positive interpretation is that Volozh and the team have created a financing flywheel in which customer demand, GPU-supplier validation, and capital access reinforce each other. The negative interpretation is that the business is already moving into a scale regime where financing architecture, dilution, debt-service capacity, and customer concentration will matter as much as engineering excellence. (SEC)
The CEO-specific investment implication is that Volozh is likely the single most important reason to own Nebius rather than a more commoditized AI infrastructure name. His record supports confidence that Nebius can compete on engineering, infrastructure efficiency, and customer credibility rather than simply buying GPUs and reselling capacity. However, Volozh is also the main reason Nebius deserves a governance discount. The optimal underwriting stance is therefore not “founder-led equals safe,” but “founder-led equals higher execution ceiling and higher governance asymmetry.” If active power, utilization, and customer diversification improve, the CEO premium can expand. If accounting controls, capex discipline, or financing quality deteriorate, the voting-control discount should widen quickly.
CFO ASSESSMENT: MARIA DEL DADO ALONSO SANCHEZ
Maria del Dado Alonso Sanchez is assessed as a strong but still unproven-in-seat CFO for Nebius, with a rating of 8/10. She became CFO effective June 2025 and brings more than 25 years of finance leadership experience across technology, consumer internet, and international growth businesses. Her background includes Group CFO roles at Berlin Brands Group and Azerion, and prior finance and controls experience at Booking.com and Amazon. This is a relevant profile for Nebius because the CFO role requires scaling finance infrastructure across jurisdictions, managing high-volume capex, integrating acquisitions, raising capital, supporting enterprise customer contracts, and improving control systems after a complex corporate separation. (SEC)
The CFO hire should be viewed as a deliberate upgrade for the next phase of Nebius’s lifecycle. Ron Jacobs was described by Nebius as having played a pivotal role during the restructuring and finance-function buildout, while Dado Alonso was positioned as a CFO with capital-markets, operational-finance, and digital-business-model experience. This handoff is logical: the finance challenge has shifted from post-Yandex separation and relisting toward multi-billion-dollar project finance, convertible issuance, customer prepayments, asset-backed structures, GPU depreciation, data-center accounting, and working-capital management. Her appointment aligns with the company’s transition from restructuring story to scaled infrastructure company. (SEC)
The early financial execution under the current finance leadership is encouraging but cannot yet be considered fully seasoned. In Q1 2026, Nebius reported $9.298B of cash and cash equivalents, $22.303B of total assets, $15.061B of total liabilities, and $8.432B of noncurrent debt. Operating cash flow from continuing operations was $2.258B, while property, equipment, and intangible-asset investments were . The company also disclosed that near-term funding sources could include cash on hand, customer prepayments, asset-backed financing, corporate-level debt, and other debt instruments, and that at-the-market equity issuance had not been used to date. This indicates a finance function capable of handling large-scale capital formation, but it also highlights the magnitude of future balance-sheet and cash-flow complexity. (SEC)
The main CFO red flag is internal control over financial reporting. Nebius disclosed material weaknesses as of December 31, 2025 relating to internal control over fixed assets and TripleTen revenue recognition, with a goal of remediation by the end of 2026. The fixed-asset weakness is particularly important for Nebius because the investment case depends heavily on capex reliability, GPU useful lives, data-center construction cost, depreciation, and capital efficiency. A material weakness in fixed assets at a company spending billions of dollars on GPUs and data centers is not a cosmetic issue. It affects confidence in capex tracking, asset capitalization, depreciation policies, impairment risk, and return-on-invested-capital analysis. The issue is not thesis-breaking if remediated on schedule, but it is a material diligence item until closed. (Stock Titan)
The depreciation-policy change is another area requiring careful monitoring. Beginning in Q1 2026, Nebius changed the estimated useful life of server and network equipment from 4 years to 5 years. This may be reasonable if management has evidence that hardware remains economically productive longer than previously assumed, especially with strong demand for AI compute. However, it also improves reported depreciation burden and margin optics relative to the prior estimate. In a business with fast-changing GPU technology, the useful-life assumption should be treated as an active underwriting variable, not an accounting footnote. The CFO’s credibility will depend on transparent disclosure around utilization, resale values, customer contract duration, maintenance capex, and any impairment indicators as newer GPU generations arrive. (SEC)
Dado Alonso’s equity ownership and trading record do not currently indicate a material alignment problem. A recent Form 4 showed a small sale of 1,509 Class A shares at approximately $276.20, made solely to cover tax-withholding obligations under automatic instructions, leaving her with 12,672 shares after the transaction. This is economically immaterial relative to Nebius’s market capitalization and should not be interpreted as discretionary negative signaling. The more important CFO-alignment issue is not open-market selling, but whether compensation, equity vesting, and control-remediation milestones are sufficiently tied to durable free cash flow, capex efficiency, customer diversification, and balance-sheet quality. (Stock Titan)
The CFO-specific investment implication is that Dado Alonso appears appropriately matched to the company’s next stage, but the burden of proof is high. The finance function must prove it can support a capital program that is much closer to hyperscale infrastructure than conventional software. The most important milestones are remediation of the fixed-asset control weakness by end-2026, clear disclosure of capex per MW and per GPU cluster, prudent management of convertible and debt maturities, disciplined SBC and dilution control, and improved transparency around customer concentration. Successful execution would materially reduce the equity risk premium. Failure would increase the probability that Nebius trades at a persistent discount to infrastructure quality despite strong revenue growth.
COO ASSESSMENT: OPHIR NAVE
Ophir Nave is assessed as a high-quality corporate-operations and transaction-execution leader, with a rating of 7.5/10. He was appointed COO in May 2024 and executive director in August 2024. His background is not the standard data-center-operations profile; he was previously lead partner in Corporate and M&A at Arnon, Tadmor-Levy, served on the firm’s executive committee, worked at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, clerked for the Israeli Supreme Court, lectured on corporate finance at Tel Aviv University, and holds an S.J.D. from Harvard, an LL.B. from Tel Aviv University, and a B.Sc. in computer engineering from the Technion. This profile is unusually strong for structuring, M&A, corporate governance, commercial contracting, and complex cross-border execution. (Stock Titan)
The COO profile is well suited to Nebius’s corporate complexity. Nebius is simultaneously managing public-company governance in the Netherlands and the U.S., large customer contracts, GPU-supplier relationships, potential project-finance structures, acquisitions such as Tavily, Eigen AI, and Clarifai, post-divestiture entity architecture, and data-center development across multiple jurisdictions. Nave’s legal, M&A, corporate-finance, and technical background is therefore directly relevant. His value is likely highest in reducing friction around strategic agreements, capital formation, entity structuring, acquisitions, and governance-sensitive transactions. (Stock Titan)
The COO red flag is that Nave is not, based on disclosed background, a career hyperscale data-center operations executive. Nebius’s most difficult operating problems over the next 2 years are likely to include power interconnection, construction sequencing, supply-chain timing, liquid cooling or other infrastructure design choices, GPU deployment, uptime, cluster reliability, and utilization ramp. Those tasks appear to rely more heavily on Andrey Korolenko, Roman Chernin, Danila Shtan, and the broader infrastructure engineering organization than on Nave personally. This is not necessarily negative, because the COO role at Nebius may be designed around corporate operating architecture rather than facilities operations. However, it means the investment case should not over-attribute physical-infrastructure execution to the COO title alone. (Stock Titan)
The COO-specific investment implication is that Nebius has a sophisticated corporate operator for structuring and transaction execution, which is valuable in a business where customer contracts, financing instruments, acquisitions, and regulatory compliance are strategically important. The offset is that the company must demonstrate depth beneath the COO in physical infrastructure execution. Evidence of timely delivery across Finland, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Missouri, Spain, and other co-location or owned sites will matter more than organizational titles. If Nebius delivers 800 MW-1 GW of connected power by year-end 2026 while maintaining margin discipline, the COO structure will be validated. If construction delays, interconnection setbacks, or operational outages occur, the market will likely focus on whether the operating model was too dependent on technical founders and too light on seasoned hyperscale facilities leadership. (SEC)
OTHER KEY SENIOR MANAGEMENT TEAM MEMBERS:
Roman Chernin, Chief Business Officer and co-founder, is one of the most important operators in the company. He leads business strategy and product direction, including Token Factory, and previously spent more than 10 years at Yandex leading Search and later Maps and Navigation. His background is a significant green flag because search and maps are infrastructure-heavy, latency-sensitive, data-intensive products requiring product discipline, monetization awareness, and large engineering-team coordination. In the Nebius context, Chernin appears to bridge product strategy, customer needs, and infrastructure economics. The investment implication is positive: Nebius’s commercial strategy is not being led solely by sales hires or finance executives; it is anchored by an operator with deep experience converting complex technical platforms into widely used products. (Stock Titan)
Andrey Korolenko, Chief Product and Infrastructure Officer and co-founder, is arguably the most strategically important non-CEO technical executive. He was previously Head of Infrastructure at Yandex and is described as having experience across hardware, software, development, construction, and operations of efficient high-performance GPU-driven data centers and related technology services. Nebius materials also cite his nearly 20 years of experience in infrastructure and supercomputer deployment. This background directly maps to Nebius’s key value drivers: data-center design, GPU cluster deployment, capacity utilization, power efficiency, and infrastructure reliability. The investment implication is that Korolenko’s presence substantially strengthens confidence in the company’s ability to build differentiated infrastructure rather than merely procure third-party capacity. (Stock Titan)
Danila Shtan, Chief Technology Officer, adds continuity in developer infrastructure and technical platform execution. He previously held senior roles in developer infrastructure and classifieds technology at Yandex. This matters because Nebius must compete not only on raw GPU availability, but also on developer experience, orchestration, reliability, scheduling, software abstraction, observability, and integration with AI workloads. CTO quality is therefore important to customer retention and pricing power. The current disclosure provides less external performance evidence for Shtan than for Volozh, Korolenko, or Chernin, but the background is directionally aligned with the product requirements of an AI cloud platform. (Stock Titan)
Marc Boroditsky, Chief Revenue Officer, is a major commercial upgrade. He joined as CRO in May 2025 after serving as President of Revenue at Cloudflare and previously holding senior revenue roles at Twilio, including SVP of Sales and CRO. Nebius’s release around the appointment highlighted that during his Twilio tenure the company’s paying customer base grew by more than 6x and revenue grew more than 10x to approximately . This is highly relevant because Nebius must move from founder-led strategic customer wins to repeatable enterprise GTM execution across AI-native companies, large enterprises, and hyperscaler-adjacent buyers. The investment implication is positive: the company has added a CRO with credible experience scaling cloud-like revenue organizations, which should help reduce dependence on a small number of strategic megadeals over time. (Stock Titan)
Boaz Tal, General Counsel, joined in January 2025 after serving as Deputy CEO and General Counsel at Israel Shipyards Industries and previously holding senior positions across legal, tax, finance, and business development functions. The GC role is non-trivial at Nebius because the company faces export-control scrutiny, AI infrastructure compliance, cross-border data-center development, customer-contract complexity, financing documentation, shareholder-governance issues, and possible M&A integration. Tal’s industrial and legal background appears relevant, though the company’s legal and compliance demands will likely increase as U.S. government, strategic-customer, and NVIDIA-linked relationships expand. (Stock Titan)
Recent go-to-market leadership additions are also relevant. Nebius disclosed new commercial leaders including Dan Lawrence as SVP and GM Americas, John Haarer as GM APJ, and Raja Agrawal as VP MEA, with prior experience across Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Twilio, SAP, Microsoft, and BrowserStack. This matters because the commercial organization must broaden beyond founder-led strategic demand and convert pipeline into durable, diversified contracted revenue. Nebius also disclosed that its customer pipeline increased 3.5x quarter over quarter and that larger deal sizes and firmer pricing were visible in the market. The quality of the GTM bench therefore has direct implications for customer concentration, utilization, and margin durability. (SEC)
The senior-management bench has a distinctive mix: technical and product depth is heavily derived from Yandex/Nebius continuity, while finance, revenue, and legal leadership have been supplemented with external executives from global technology, cloud, e-commerce, legal, and industrial backgrounds. This is generally positive. The green flag is that the company has not attempted to solve a hyperscale-infrastructure problem with a purely financial team. The red flag is that several core executives share common institutional roots, which may create cultural cohesion but also increases the risk of groupthink, operating assumptions imported from prior environments, and insufficient challenge around U.S.-scale power, permitting, customer procurement, and public-company controls. The investment case requires both continuity and externalization; current hiring suggests progress, but the operating record is still short.
BOARD, GOVERNANCE AND CONTROL:
Nebius’s board structure is adequate but not best-in-class for minority shareholders. The board includes John Boynton as chairman, Elena Bunina, Arne Grimme, Kira Radinsky, Charles Ryan, Matt Weigand, Arkady Volozh, and Ophir Nave. The board includes relevant technology, venture, finance, M&A, scientific, and legal expertise. Ryan chairs the audit committee and is identified as an audit committee financial expert; the audit committee consists of Ryan, Boynton, and Weigand and is fully independent. The compensation committee consists of Radinsky, Boynton, and Weigand and is also fully independent. These are meaningful mitigants to the controlled-company structure. (Stock Titan)
The governance weakness is the nomination and governance committee. It consists of Volozh, Boynton, and Radinsky, is only majority independent, and is chaired by Volozh. Nebius relies on the Nasdaq controlled-company exemption for this structure. From an investment perspective, this is the wrong committee to have founder dominance if the concern is long-term board independence, succession planning, or CEO accountability. The company’s disclosure also states that Volozh beneficially holds approximately 52% of the voting power, which makes external challenge structurally limited. This does not negate the operating quality of the team, but it increases the required margin of safety for governance-sensitive investors. (Stock Titan)
Board composition provides some substantive positives. Kira Radinsky brings AI, predictive analytics, healthcare technology, and entrepreneurial experience; Charles Ryan brings capital markets, investment banking, and Russia/Eastern Europe transaction experience; Matt Weigand brings venture and growth-investing experience through Accel; Arne Grimme brings Dutch M&A and legal expertise; and John Boynton provides long-term company continuity. The board therefore appears better suited than a generic public-company board to evaluate AI infrastructure, venture-style scaling, complex capital structures, and cross-border transactions. However, long-tenured relationships and founder voting control reduce the degree to which the board can be treated as an independent disciplining mechanism. (Stock Titan)
A minor but relevant governance disclosure is that Elena Bunina and Roman Chernin are married. This does not imply a governance failure and is transparently disclosed, but it is part of the broader pattern of close historical and personal ties within the Nebius/Yandex talent network. Such ties can improve trust and speed in a technically complex business, but they can also reduce perceived independence. For valuation, the more important issue remains founder voting control rather than any 1 relationship. (Stock Titan)
COMPENSATION, OWNERSHIP AND INCENTIVE ALIGNMENT:
Nebius’s compensation disclosure is consistent with foreign private issuer-style reporting and is less granular than a U.S. domestic proxy. This limits the ability to evaluate named-executive target pay, annual bonus metrics, individual performance goals, and relative peer benchmarking. For 2025, aggregate cash compensation for senior management was $5.9M across 8 people, and senior management received 6,350,000 share options and 226,312 RSUs. The awards generally vest over 4 years in quarterly installments. Non-executive directors received $0.9M of aggregate cash compensation and 27,198 RSUs. The structure is therefore heavily equity-oriented at the senior-management level. (Stock Titan)
The 2025 option grants are especially important. Nebius disclosed that 6,350,000 options were granted in 2025 at a weighted-average exercise price of $96.69, that 6,000,000 of these options included market conditions, and that 6,000,000 options with a $100 exercise price were outstanding at year-end 2025. These 6,000,000 options represent approximately 2.4% of the 253.9M shares outstanding as of March 31, 2026, before considering other plan dilution. The premium-priced, market-conditioned structure is directionally shareholder-aligned because it requires material share-price appreciation and continued service. It is superior to deeply in-the-money grants or low-hurdle time-based RSUs, particularly in a company where management execution is the central asset. (Stock Titan)
The CEO’s treatment of the 2025 premium-priced option program is a notable alignment signal. Nebius’s 2024 disclosure indicated that the board approved $100 premium-priced options for up to 4 senior executives, including the CEO, but that Volozh declined to participate. This reduces incremental CEO dilution and is consistent with a founder already having substantial economic and voting exposure. However, Volozh’s control position also means the alignment analysis is not straightforward. A founder with approximately 52% voting control and a much lower economic interest has strong reputational and strategic alignment, but the voting/economic divergence can create minority-shareholder risk if strategic priorities diverge from per-share value maximization. (SEC)
The 2024 compensation year was distorted by the extraordinary restructuring context. Senior-management cash compensation was $14.9M for 9 people, including $7.8M of cash paid in lieu of equity awards and repurchases that could not occur while Nasdaq trading was suspended. Non-executive director compensation was also unusually elevated, including special bonuses related to the complexity of the divestment and restructuring process. These payments should not be extrapolated as normal-course recurring compensation. However, they do show that the board was willing to pay significant one-time rewards for transaction execution. That is defensible given the successful separation of non-Russian assets, but it reinforces the need to monitor compensation governance now that Nebius is operating as a scaled listed AI infrastructure company rather than a restructuring vehicle. (SEC)
The equity plan is broad and potentially dilutive. The plan permits options, SARs, restricted shares, RSUs, PSUs, business-unit awards, and subsidiary-level awards. The maximum share availability is approximately 33M shares, equal to roughly 13.0% of the 253.9M shares outstanding as of March 31, 2026. Business-unit awards can also be issued in participating subsidiaries, currently including Avride, with awards per subsidiary capped at up to 20% of that subsidiary’s shares. The plan does not permit repricing without shareholder approval except in major capital events, which is a positive governance feature. The investment implication is that equity compensation is appropriate for talent retention in AI infrastructure, but dilution must be actively modeled, especially because Nebius competes for talent against U.S. AI infrastructure companies, venture-backed AI platforms, and hyperscalers. (Stock Titan)
Relative to AI infrastructure peers and hyperscaler-adjacent talent markets, Nebius’s pay design appears strategically rational. The company competes with cloud providers and GPU-capacity platforms including AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Together.ai, DeepInfra, and others. Competing against that labor market with conventional European cash pay would be unrealistic. Large equity awards, premium-priced options, and long vesting are commercially sensible tools to retain technical, infrastructure, and GTM talent. The risk is that compensation disclosure remains insufficiently detailed for U.S.-style governance analysis, and the combination of founder control plus broad equity-plan authority could weaken shareholder oversight if dilution accelerates. (SEC)
Share-based compensation is already economically meaningful. Nebius reported $35.3M of share-based compensation in Q1 2026, representing 7% of operating expenses. At the current scale, this is manageable and not unusual for a high-growth technology company. However, because Nebius is both capital-intensive and equity-compensation-intensive, dilution and SBC cannot be ignored as secondary issues. A software company with high SBC may still convert to high free cash flow as it scales; an AI infrastructure company with high SBC and multi-billion-dollar capex must prove that equity issuance, debt, customer prepayments, and depreciation all translate into attractive per-share returns. (SEC)
INTERNAL CONTROLS, FINANCE QUALITY AND ACCOUNTING RISK:
The most important finance-quality concern is the material weakness in fixed-asset controls. For a business whose investment case is built around GPUs, data centers, and power infrastructure, fixed-asset accounting is central to understanding the business. Errors in fixed-asset tracking can affect capitalization, depreciation, impairments, reported margins, asset utilization, and capital efficiency. Nebius’s goal of remediation by end-2026 is important, but until remediation is complete, a higher evidentiary burden should be applied to management’s capex and margin disclosures. The issue is manageable if transparently remediated; it would become thesis-damaging if repeated beyond 2026 or accompanied by restatements, impairments, or unexplained capex variance. (Stock Titan)
The TripleTen revenue-recognition weakness is less central to the AI Cloud thesis but still relevant to broader finance discipline. TripleTen is not the primary valuation driver, but revenue-recognition weaknesses at any subsidiary raise questions about finance-system integration, ERP maturity, contract review, and control culture after the corporate separation. The appropriate interpretation is not that Nebius’s AI Cloud revenue is necessarily unreliable, but that the finance organization is still maturing while the operating scale is accelerating rapidly. This mismatch between control maturity and capital-program scale is one of the most important management-risk variables. (Stock Titan)
The customer and supplier concentration disclosures also elevate the importance of management judgment. Nebius disclosed significant customer concentration in accounts receivable, with one customer representing 83% of accounts receivable at year-end 2025, and disclosed that 2025 capital expenditures were concentrated with 2 suppliers. This is not surprising for an AI infrastructure company in a market dominated by large strategic buyers and constrained GPU supply. It is also not benign. Concentration can validate demand and strengthen financing access, but it can also reduce pricing power, increase working-capital volatility, and create counterparty-specific risk. Management must prove that strategic deals with Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and other major partners create durable economics rather than dependency. (Stock Titan)
CULTURE, TALENT AND ORGANIZATIONAL SCALING:
Nebius’s culture appears engineering-led, founder-driven, and technically deep. This is a major positive in AI infrastructure, where the gap between a real platform and a GPU-broker model can be decisive. The company’s roots in Yandex infrastructure, search, maps, developer tools, and machine learning provide a coherent talent base. Nebius also appears to be externalizing the management team by adding executives with Amazon, Booking.com, Cloudflare, Twilio, SAP, Microsoft, Akamai, AWS, BrowserStack, and legal/industrial backgrounds. This combination of internal technical continuity and external commercial/finance capabilities is directionally strong. (Stock Titan)
The scaling burden is significant. Employee count increased from 1,195 at year-end 2024 to 1,543 at year-end 2025. U.S. headcount increased from 171 to 351, Netherlands headcount increased from 474 to 584, and total product-development headcount increased from 653 to 813. SG&A headcount increased from 430 to 580. This hiring pattern is consistent with the shift from R&D and restructuring toward commercial scaling, finance, infrastructure operations, and public-company execution. The positive interpretation is that Nebius is investing ahead of a large contracted-demand opportunity. The negative interpretation is that the organization is scaling across geographies, functions, and acquired assets before finance controls have fully matured. (Stock Titan)
Employee relations appear stable based on disclosed information. Nebius disclosed no collective-bargaining agreements, no work stoppages, a Dutch works council, and management’s belief that employee relations are good. In an engineering-led infrastructure company, retention risk is more likely to come from equity-market volatility, competition from hyperscalers, founder-culture strain, or integration complexity than from traditional labor conflict. The primary culture diligence item is therefore talent retention among the core Yandex/Nebius infrastructure leaders and successful integration of U.S. GTM and data-center execution talent. (Stock Titan)
GREEN FLAGS:
The strongest management green flag is founder-led technical credibility. Volozh, Chernin, Korolenko, and Shtan collectively give Nebius a management DNA that is materially more technical than most public-company infrastructure roll-ups. This matters because AI cloud economics are driven by utilization, cluster efficiency, software abstraction, customer reliability, power cost, procurement discipline, and engineering iteration speed. A management team that understands the stack from hardware and data-center design through software and customer workflows is more likely to avoid commoditized returns. (Stock Titan)
The 2nd green flag is strategic validation. NVIDIA’s investment, the NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud designation, the Meta agreement, and the Microsoft relationship materially reduce the probability that Nebius is merely a promotional AI infrastructure story. These relationships do not eliminate margin or financing risk, but they validate the platform’s relevance to sophisticated counterparties. The market should treat these partnerships as a meaningful management scorecard item because strategic customers and suppliers conduct diligence that public investors cannot fully replicate. (SEC)
The 3rd green flag is speed of execution. Nebius moved from post-divestiture repositioning into rapid AI Cloud revenue growth, large-scale contracted power procurement, strategic financing, and major customer agreements within a short period. Q1 2026 revenue growth, AI Cloud margin, capital raised, and contracted-capacity disclosures all indicate management is operating with urgency and credibility. In a market where GPU supply, power access, and customer demand are time-sensitive, speed is itself a competitive advantage. (SEC)
The 4th green flag is the structure of senior-management incentives. The large $100 premium-priced option grants with market conditions create meaningful upside alignment and are more attractive than low-hurdle RSU-heavy compensation. Volozh’s decision to decline the CEO allocation of those options is also positive from a dilution and optics standpoint. The compensation structure appears designed to reward large value creation rather than ordinary retention alone. (SEC)
RED FLAGS:
The most important red flag is governance control. Volozh’s 52% voting control and the company’s controlled-company status reduce external governance leverage. This matters because Nebius is entering a period in which management will make high-stakes decisions around leverage, dilution, customer concentration, capex sequencing, acquisitions, and geographic expansion. If these decisions succeed, control will be viewed as enabling speed. If they fail, control will be viewed as entrenchment. (Stock Titan)
The 2nd red flag is internal-control maturity. The fixed-asset material weakness is particularly relevant because fixed assets are the core of the business model. In a lower-capex software company, such a weakness might be secondary. At Nebius, it sits directly at the center of the investment debate. It affects confidence in reported capital efficiency and depreciation assumptions, and it is especially important after the useful-life change from 4 years to 5 years for server and network equipment. (Stock Titan)
The 3rd red flag is execution complexity. Nebius is pursuing one of the most demanding operating models in public technology markets: multi-GW power procurement, global data-center development, GPU supply-chain management, enterprise AI customer acquisition, capital-market financing, and software-platform differentiation. Even an excellent management team can fail if interconnection timelines, construction costs, cooling design, GPU supply, customer demand, or financing terms move adversely. Management quality improves the odds, but the operating model remains structurally unforgiving. (SEC)
The 4th red flag is concentration risk. Large strategic customers are a validation signal, but they can also become a risk if revenue, receivables, utilization, or financing assumptions depend on a small number of counterparties. Supplier concentration is similarly understandable in a GPU-constrained market but exposes the company to supply timing, pricing, allocation, and technology-transition risk. Nebius’s management team must therefore be judged not only by headline contract value, but by customer diversification, realized utilization, pricing durability, and supplier optionality. (Stock Titan)
INVESTMENT IMPLICATIONS:
Management quality is a clear positive factor in the long thesis. The company has a credible founder-operator, technically strong infrastructure leadership, an upgraded CFO, a commercially credible CRO, and strategic counterparties that provide external validation. This supports the view that Nebius is one of the more credible public-market AI infrastructure platforms. The management team increases the probability that the company can build real infrastructure, win strategic customers, and operate differentiated AI cloud capacity rather than compete purely on price.
The equity should nevertheless be treated as a high-beta execution vehicle rather than a fully de-risked compounder. Revenue growth and contracted capacity are exceptionally strong, but the model requires continuous successful conversion of capital into deployed capacity, deployed capacity into utilized compute, and utilized compute into attractive returns on capital. The management team has earned a degree of credibility, but the business is still in the phase where errors compound quickly. A 6-month construction delay, a GPU underutilization cycle, a failed control remediation, or a customer-concentration surprise could materially alter the risk/reward.
The valuation framework should assign management a positive execution premium but apply a governance and control discount. Volozh’s founder leadership and technical record justify higher confidence than would be appropriate for a newly assembled financial-sponsor-style management team. However, his voting control, the controlled-company exemption, and limited minority-shareholder influence should reduce the governance multiple. In practical terms, management quality should raise the probability of upside realization but should not lower the required return to the level of a mature, independently governed hyperscaler.
The key long-side catalyst path is milestone-based. The most important milestones are 800 MW-1 GW of connected power by year-end 2026, more than 4 GW of contracted capacity, continued conversion of the Meta and Microsoft commitments into revenue, sustained AI Cloud adjusted EBITDA margin, customer-pipeline conversion, successful financing without excessive dilution, and remediation of internal-control weaknesses by end-2026. If those milestones are achieved, management credibility will increase sharply and the equity can re-rate on reduced execution risk. (SEC)
The key short-side or risk-management thesis is also management-linked. If the market begins to question capex discipline, useful-life assumptions, customer concentration, internal controls, or financing quality, Nebius could de-rate rapidly even if headline revenue remains high. The stock’s downside risk would be particularly acute if operating momentum slows before the company proves durable returns on deployed capital. In that scenario, high founder control would become a liability because external governance remedies would be limited.
Activist involvement is structurally unlikely to be a primary investment catalyst. Volozh’s voting control means any governance-driven restructuring, management replacement, sale process, or board refresh would likely require founder alignment. This reduces the probability of activist downside protection. The practical implication is that Nebius should not be underwritten as a governance-improvement or management-change story. It should be underwritten as a founder-led execution story in which the existing management team either creates the value or the thesis weakens materially.
M&A optionality is strategically plausible but governance-constrained. Nebius could be valuable to hyperscalers, GPU suppliers, sovereign AI initiatives, or infrastructure investors because of its contracted power, technical team, customer base, and AI Cloud platform. However, the dual-class founder-control structure makes a hostile or externally forced transaction improbable. Any strategic transaction would likely require Volozh’s support. This limits takeover optionality as an independent valuation floor, but it does not eliminate strategic scarcity value.
The most important diligence items going forward are management-specific. The first is whether Dado Alonso remediates the fixed-asset and revenue-recognition weaknesses by end-2026. The 2nd is whether Korolenko and the infrastructure team deliver connected and active power on schedule. The 3rd is whether Boroditsky and the expanded GTM organization diversify revenue beyond a small number of strategic customers. The 4th is whether Volozh maintains capital discipline as available financing expands. The 5th is whether SBC, equity-plan dilution, convertibles, and debt remain proportionate to realized per-share value creation.
BOTTOM LINE:
Nebius has an unusually strong management team for a public AI infrastructure company, led by a proven founder with a rare combination of technical, product, infrastructure, and capital-markets relevance. The CEO and technical bench are major positives. The CFO hire is appropriate for the capital-intensive scaling phase, but the finance organization must prove control maturity. The COO is highly credible for transactions, governance, and corporate execution, though physical infrastructure delivery depends heavily on the technical infrastructure leaders beneath and around him. Compensation is broadly aligned through substantial equity and premium-priced options, but disclosure is less granular than a U.S. proxy and dilution must be modeled carefully. Governance is the largest structural weakness because founder voting control materially limits minority-shareholder influence. Overall, management should be treated as a positive differentiator and a legitimate reason to underwrite a more ambitious growth path than for lower-quality AI infrastructure peers. The same management structure also creates higher governance asymmetry, making the equity highly dependent on continued execution, transparent controls, disciplined financing, and visible conversion of contracted capacity into attractive per-share economics.

The script currently evaluates multiple distinct triggers. Strict structural safeguards include:

(Phase 13 Update: Long Puts / Tail Hedges are now correctly programmed to calculate $0 in locked margin to align with regulatory cash-settlement rules and prevent artificial drift).
•	[ACTIVE] Naked Options: The sync_engine_v19.py utilizes qualifyContracts() to unpack opaque IBKR BAG (Combo) orders into their explicit option legs. The system accurately maps resting OCO brackets and reliably warns the CIO of exposed flanks.
•	[ACTIVE] TOR Capacity Breach: The dashboard continuously aggregates the absolute USD risk of all active Stop-Losses across all silos, converting it into a "Global TOR" metric (weighed against the Master Estate NAV). It cross-references this active exposure against the algorithmic Market Regime (Green/Yellow/Red). If Active Global TOR exceeds the Regime's optimal limit (e.g., > 4.0 R in a Green Regime), it blares a red alert commanding the CIO to mechanically raise stops to break-even or scale out of positions.
•	21-DTE Gamma Cliff Protocol: The dashboard now actively hunts for short option contracts reaching 21 Days to Expiration. It fires a yellow warning at 30 DTE, and a CRITICAL red alert at <= 21 DTE, commanding the CIO to mechanically eject and avoid explosive terminal Gamma risk.
•	API Redundancy Fallback: The dashboard now features a local SQLite fallback database. If yfinance crashes or rate-limits the Estate, the dashboard will silently switch to cached FX rates, IRX yields, and Benchmark data to prevent the Total Open Risk (TOR) math and GAAP reporting from failing.
###
Addendum 2: The IBKR "Double Negative" Combo Logic Trap (UPDATED)
One of the most dangerous operational hazards we navigate is Interactive Brokers' highly counterintuitive "double negative" order routing for complex options combinations. If an incoming portfolio manager does not understand this mechanic, they risk accidentally doubling the Estate's market exposure or triggering silent order rejections when attempting to set risk-management brackets.
1. The Root Cause of the Confusion & The "Single Leg" Exception
When you use the TWS Strategy Builder to construct a spread (whether it is a Bull Put or a Bear Call), IBKR stops treating the legs as individual options. Instead, it packages them together into a single, synthetic asset called a "Combo." Because we act as the "Casino" selling insurance, our goal is always to collect a net credit upfront. However, IBKR represents a "Credit" as a negative price.
•	The Combo Golden Rule (For VRP Spreads):
o	BUYING a negative number = Receiving Cash (Credit).
o	SELLING a negative number = Paying Cash (Debit).
•	The Single-Leg Exception (For Tail Hedges):
o	Deep OTM Tail Hedges are single-leg options, not Combos. Therefore, they behave normally. To deploy a Tail Hedge, you submit a standard BUY order at a POSITIVE limit price (paying cash/debit).
2. The Bull Put Case
When establishing Bull Put Spreads, here is how the logic flows:
•	Opening the Trade: To collect a $2.38 premium, we must submit a BUY order for the combo at a Limit Price of -2.38 C. By "Buying" a negative number, the broker deposits $2.38 per share into our account. Because we "Bought" the combo to open it, the TWS portfolio officially lists us as holding a Long position in that specific synthetic asset.
•	Closing the Trade: Because we hold a Long position in the combo, we must execute a SELL order to close it. Our 50% Take-Profit target requires a Limit Price of -1.19 D. By "Selling" a negative number, we pay cash (a Debit) to buy back the legs.
3. The Bear Call Case
The exact same logic applies to Bear Call Spreads. Even though we are fundamentally "Selling Calls" to open a Bear Call spread, the TWS Strategy Builder packages it as a Combo. To collect our premium, we must still BUY the combo at a negative limit price. This once again gives us a Long position in the synthetic Bear Call asset, meaning we must SELL it to close the position.
4. The "Rejected Stop-Loss" Trap & The Execution Ban
Interactive Brokers' routing engine frequently rejects standard Stop (STP) orders on multi-leg Combos (turning them Red in the TWS status column). This occurs because complex spreads suffer from wide bid/ask quoting, making traditional stop triggers unreliable.
•	The Hazard: If a manager uses the native TWS 'Attach Bracket' tool or submits a standard STP for an OCO bracket, IBKR may silently kill the order, leaving the Estate completely naked to downside risk.
•	The Execution Ban: Never use the native TWS "Attach Bracket" tool or standard STP orders for multi-leg Combos.
5. The Official Solution: The Foolproof OCA Protocol
As of Phase 13, all managers must strictly execute closing brackets using The Foolproof OCA Protocol, which has been officially codified into The Official XSP / XND Entry Rules (v6).
Protective stops and take-profits for Combos MUST be constructed as two independent, standalone closing orders:
1.	The Take Profit: A standard Limit (LMT) closing order.
2.	The Stop-Loss: A Market (MKT) closing order, held locally on IBKR's servers via the TWS "Conditional" tab. The execution condition must be tied directly to the highly liquid underlying index (e.g., "Trigger this order if XSP Index drops <= 704").
3.	The Link: Both independent orders are linked flawlessly by typing a matching, unique identifier into the 'OCA Group' (One Cancels All) field located in the Comprehensive 'Misc' tab of the Order Ticket.
6. The Final Warning for the Incoming Manager
The incoming manager must always look at the letter trailing the price in the TWS Order Confirmation screen:
•	"C" (Credit): Cash is entering the Estate. This should only happen on the opening trade.
•	"D" (Debit): Cash is leaving the Estate. This should only happen on the closing trade (Take-Profit or Stop-Loss).
If the manager accidentally sets the OCO trap as a "BUY" order, or forgets the negative signs, they will inadvertently open a second, identical spread, doubling the Estate's risk exposure instead of closing it out!
•	The Exception for Alpha Equities: While multi-leg options cannot use native TWS Stop (STP) orders due to rejection traps, Alpha assets (individual Stocks/CFDs) MUST use native TWS STP orders. The dashboard's Champion Journal engine actively hunts the TWS order book for these resting STP orders to dynamically calculate the live "Open Risk (R)" for Panel 10. Without a native STP order, the dashboard will assume $0.00 stop distance and report 100% of the position value as catastrophic Open Risk.

"""
def load_and_process_data():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
    df = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM daily_balances", conn)
    df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])
    
    # Preserve legacy manual SQL patches from 'total_cash'
    df.rename(columns={'net_liquidation': 'nav', 'total_cash': 'legacy_flow'}, inplace=True)
    
    try:
        transfers_df = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM cash_transfers", conn)
        transfers_df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(transfers_df['date'])
        daily_transfers = transfers_df.groupby(['date', 'account'])['amount'].sum().reset_index()
        daily_transfers.rename(columns={'amount': 'new_flow'}, inplace=True)
        df = pd.merge(df, daily_transfers, on=['date', 'account'], how='left')
        df['new_flow'] = df['new_flow'].fillna(0.0)
    except Exception:
        df['new_flow'] = 0.0
        
    # Combine legacy SQL patches with new UI ledger entries
    df['legacy_flow'] = df['legacy_flow'].fillna(0.0)
    df['net_flow'] = df['legacy_flow'] + df['new_flow']
    
    global_df = df.groupby('date').agg({'nav': 'sum', 'net_flow': 'sum'}).reset_index()
    global_metrics = process_metrics(global_df, LIVE_RF_RATE)
    global_df = global_df[global_df['nav'] > 0].copy() 
    
    silo_metrics = {}
    silo_dfs = {}
    for acc in SILO_MAP.keys():
        acc_df = df[df['account'] == acc].copy().sort_values('date')
        silo_metrics[acc] = process_metrics(acc_df, LIVE_RF_RATE)
        acc_df = acc_df[acc_df['nav'] > 0].copy()
        if not acc_df.empty:
            acc_df['prev_nav'] = acc_df['nav'].shift(1)
            acc_df['daily_return'] = (acc_df['nav'] - acc_df['net_flow'] - acc_df['prev_nav']) / acc_df['prev_nav'].replace(0, np.nan)
            acc_df['cum_return'] = (1 + acc_df['daily_return'].fillna(0)).cumprod() - 1
            acc_df['daily_pnl'] = acc_df['nav'] - acc_df['net_flow'] - acc_df['prev_nav'].fillna(acc_df['nav'] - acc_df['net_flow'])
        silo_dfs[acc] = acc_df

    # Global tracking arrays (now using True PnL)
    if not global_df.empty:
        global_df['prev_nav'] = global_df['nav'].shift(1)
        global_df['daily_return'] = (global_df['nav'] - global_df['net_flow'] - global_df['prev_nav']) / global_df['prev_nav'].replace(0, np.nan)
        global_df['cum_return'] = (1 + global_df['daily_return'].fillna(0)).cumprod() - 1
        global_df['daily_pnl'] = global_df['nav'] - global_df['net_flow'] - global_df['prev_nav'].fillna(global_df['nav'] - global_df['net_flow'])
        global_df['cum_pnl'] = global_df['daily_pnl'].cumsum()

    live_date = df['date'].max()
    pos_df = pd.read_sql_query(f"SELECT account, symbol, sec_type, position, market_price, market_value, avg_cost, unrealized_pnl FROM daily_positions WHERE date = '{live_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}'", conn)
    attr_df = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM daily_attribution", conn)
    if not attr_df.empty: attr_df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(attr_df['date'])
    
    try: open_orders_df = pd.read_sql_query(f"SELECT * FROM open_orders WHERE date = '{live_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}'", conn)
    except: open_orders_df = pd.DataFrame()
        
    def categorize(sym, sec, pos):
        s = sym.upper()
        if 'IB01' in s: return 'IB01'
        if 'CSPX' in s: return 'CSPX'
        if 'CNDX' in s or 'CSNDX' in s: return 'CNDX'
        if 'ETHE' in s or 'BTC' in s: return 'Crypto'
        if 'SGLN' in s or 'IGLN' in s: return 'Gold' 
        if 'ITWN' in s: return 'ITWN'
        if 'CSKR' in s: return 'CSKR'
        if 'CNYA' in s: return 'CNYA'
        if sec == 'CASH' or 'CASH' in s: return 'Cash'
        if sec == 'CFD': return 'US Tech CFDs'
        if sec == 'STK' and not any(x in s for x in ['IB01','CSPX','CNDX','SGLN','IGLN','ITWN','CSKR','CNYA']): return 'International Stocks'
        if sec == 'OPT':
            if pos > 0: 
                try:
                    parts = s.split('_')
                    if len(parts) >= 4:
                        right = parts[3]
                        exp_date = pd.to_datetime(parts[1])
                        dte = (exp_date - pd.Timestamp.today()).days
                        if right == 'P' and dte > 60:
                            # v63: Broad Market Whitelist prevents Decapitation Bug for Sector Shorts (like SMH)
                            if parts[0] in ['SPY', 'SPX', 'XSP', 'QQQ', 'NDX', 'XND']:
                                return 'Tail Hedge'
                        elif right == 'C' and dte > 90:
                            return 'Synthetic Beta'
                except: pass
            return 'Opt Liab'
        return 'Active Swing'
    
    pos_df['asset_class'] = pos_df.apply(lambda r: categorize(r['symbol'], r['sec_type'], r['position']), axis=1)

    live_date = df['date'].max()
    pos_df = pd.read_sql_query(f"SELECT account, symbol, sec_type, position, market_price, market_value, avg_cost, unrealized_pnl, currency FROM daily_positions WHERE date = '{live_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}'", conn)
    attr_df = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM daily_attribution", conn)
    if not attr_df.empty: attr_df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(attr_df['date'])
    
    try: open_orders_df = pd.read_sql_query(f"SELECT * FROM open_orders WHERE date = '{live_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}'", conn)
    except: open_orders_df = pd.DataFrame()
        
    def categorize(sym, sec, pos, curr):
        s = sym.upper()
        if 'IB01' in s: return 'IB01'
        if 'CSPX' in s: return 'CSPX'
        if 'CNDX' in s or 'CSNDX' in s: return 'CNDX'
        if 'ETHE' in s or 'BTC' in s: return 'Crypto'
        if 'SGLN' in s or 'IGLN' in s: return 'Gold' 
        if 'ITWN' in s: return 'ITWN'
        if 'CSKR' in s: return 'CSKR'
        if 'CNYA' in s: return 'CNYA'
        if sec == 'CASH' or 'CASH' in s: return 'Cash'
        if sec == 'CFD': return 'US Tech CFDs'
        if sec == 'STK' and not any(x in s for x in ['IB01','CSPX','CNDX','SGLN','IGLN','ITWN','CSKR','CNYA']):
            # Dynamically checks the native currency from the DB schema
            return 'Physical US Stocks' if curr == 'USD' else 'International Stocks'
        if sec == 'OPT':
            if pos > 0: 
                try:
                    parts = s.split('_')
                    if len(parts) >= 4:
                        right = parts[3]
                        exp_date = pd.to_datetime(parts[1])
                        dte = (exp_date - pd.Timestamp.today()).days
                        if right == 'P' and dte > 60:
                            # v63: Broad Market Whitelist prevents Decapitation Bug for Sector Shorts (like SMH)
                            if parts[0] in ['SPY', 'SPX', 'XSP', 'QQQ', 'NDX', 'XND']:
                                return 'Tail Hedge'
                        elif right == 'C' and dte > 90:
                            return 'Synthetic Beta'
                except: pass
            return 'Opt Liab'
        return 'Active Swing'
        
    pos_df['asset_class'] = pos_df.apply(lambda r: categorize(r['symbol'], r['sec_type'], r['position'], r['currency']), axis=1)
    
    conn.close()    
    return global_df, global_metrics, silo_dfs, silo_metrics, pos_df, attr_df, df, open_orders_df

st.subheader("9B. The Options Performance Ledger & Topography Engine")

if not journal_raw_df.empty:
    
    # Generate CSV data for the full historical ledger
    csv_data = journal_raw_df.to_csv(index=False).encode('utf-8')
    st.download_button(
        label="💾 Download Full Options Journal (CSV)",
        data=csv_data,
        file_name=f"Estate_Options_Journal_{datetime.date.today().isoformat()}.csv",
        mime="text/csv"
    )

    active_vrp = journal_raw_df[pd.isnull(journal_raw_df['Close Date'])].copy()
    if not active_vrp.empty:
        active_vrp['Days Remaining'] = pd.to_numeric(active_vrp['Days Remaining'], errors='coerce')
        
        # v63: Dynamically map LIVE TWS PnL to calculate Live Annualized ROC
        live_roc_list = []
        live_ann_roc_list = []
        
        for idx, r in active_vrp.iterrows():
            try:
                tckr = str(r['Ticker']).upper()
                tranche = str(r.get('Tranche ID', ''))
                acc = 'U23144948' if 'Silo A' in tranche else ('U23154199' if 'Silo C' in tranche else None)
                
                if acc and not pos_df.empty:
                    mask = (pos_df['account'] == acc) & pos_df['symbol'].str.contains(tckr)
                    k_s = r.get('Short Strike')
                    k_l = r.get('Long Strike')
                    
                    dte_rem = float(r.get('Days Remaining', 0)) if str(r.get('Days Remaining')) != 'Closed' else 0
                    
                    sub = pos_df[mask].copy()
                    live_pnl = 0.0
                    if not sub.empty:
                        sub['exp_str'] = sub['symbol'].apply(lambda x: x.split('_')[1] if len(x.split('_'))>1 else '')
                        sub['strike_val'] = sub['symbol'].apply(lambda x: float(x.split('_')[2]) if len(x.split('_'))>2 else 0.0)
                        
                        best_exp = None
                        min_diff = 9999
                        for exp, group in sub.groupby('exp_str'):
                            strikes = group['strike_val'].tolist()
                            has_s = (pd.isna(k_s) or k_s == 0) or any(abs(s - float(k_s)) < 0.1 for s in strikes)
                            has_l = (pd.isna(k_l) or k_l == 0) or any(abs(s - float(k_l)) < 0.1 for s in strikes)
                            
                            if has_s and has_l:
                                try:
                                    exp_dt = pd.to_datetime(exp)
                                    diff = abs((exp_dt - pd.Timestamp.today()).days - dte_rem)
                                    if diff < min_diff:
                                        min_diff = diff
                                        best_exp = exp
                                except: pass
                                
                        if best_exp:
                            group = sub[sub['exp_str'] == best_exp]
                            valid_strikes = []
                            if pd.notna(k_s) and k_s > 0: valid_strikes.append(float(k_s))
                            if pd.notna(k_l) and k_l > 0: valid_strikes.append(float(k_l))
                            live_pnl = group[group['strike_val'].isin(valid_strikes)]['unrealized_pnl'].sum()
                        
                    margin = r.get('Collateral Locked (USD)', 0)
                    if pd.isna(margin) or margin <= 0:

                        margin = abs(r.get('Premium Collected (USD)', 0) * 100 * r.get('Quantity', 1))
                        
                    days_in = max(1, r.get('Days in Trade', 1))
                    
                    roc = (live_pnl / margin * 100) if margin > 0 else 0
                    ann_roc = roc * (365.0 / days_in)
                    
                    live_roc_list.append(roc)
                    live_ann_roc_list.append(ann_roc)
                else:
                    live_roc_list.append(0)
                    live_ann_roc_list.append(0)
            except:
                live_roc_list.append(0)
                live_ann_roc_list.append(0)
                
        active_vrp['Live ROC %'] = live_roc_list
        active_vrp['Live Ann ROC %'] = live_ann_roc_list

@st.cache_data(ttl=86400) # Cache for 24 hours to prevent spamming Yahoo
def get_sector(symbol, asset_class):
    # Only fetch sectors for Alpha Equities
    if asset_class not in ['Physical US Stocks', 'International Stocks', 'US Tech CFDs']:
        return asset_class
        
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
    c = conn.cursor()
    c.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS asset_sectors (symbol TEXT PRIMARY KEY, sector TEXT)")
    c.execute("SELECT sector FROM asset_sectors WHERE symbol=?", (symbol,))
    row = c.fetchone()
    
    if row:
        conn.close()
        return row[0]
        
    # Clean the ticker for Yahoo Finance (removes IBKR local exchange tags like 'TSE' or 'HEX')
    clean_sym = symbol.split()[0] 
    try:
        info = yf.Ticker(clean_sym).info
        sector = info.get('sector', 'Unknown Equities')
    except:
        sector = 'Unknown Equities'
        
    c.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO asset_sectors VALUES (?, ?)", (symbol, sector))
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()
    return sector

        except Exception:
            global_df['daily_return'] = (global_df['nav'] - global_df['net_flow'] - global_df['prev_nav']) / global_df['prev_nav'].replace(0, np.nan)
            global_df['daily_pnl'] = global_df['nav'] - global_df['net_flow'] - global_df['prev_nav'].fillna(global_df['nav'] - global_df['net_flow'])

        global_df['cum_return'] = (1 + global_df['daily_return'].fillna(0)).cumprod() - 1
        global_df['cum_pnl'] = global_df['daily_pnl'].cumsum()

    live_date = df['date'].max()
    
    # Query ONLY ONCE using the version that includes the 'currency' column
    pos_df = pd.read_sql_query(f"SELECT account, symbol, sec_type, position, market_price, market_value, avg_cost, unrealized_pnl, currency FROM daily_positions WHERE date = '{live_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}'", conn)
    
    attr_df = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM daily_attribution", conn)
    if not attr_df.empty: 
        attr_df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(attr_df['date'])
        attr_df = attr_df[attr_df['date'] >= pd.to_datetime('2025-01-01')].copy()
    
    try: open_orders_df = pd.read_sql_query(f"SELECT * FROM open_orders WHERE date = '{live_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}'", conn)
    except: open_orders_df = pd.DataFrame()
    
def categorize(sym, sec, pos, curr):
    s = sym.upper()
    if 'IB01' in s: return 'IB01'
    if 'CSPX' in s: return 'CSPX'
    if 'CNDX' in s or 'CSNDX' in s: return 'CNDX'
    if 'ETHE' in s or 'BTC' in s: return 'Crypto'
    if 'SGLN' in s or 'IGLN' in s: return 'Gold' 
    if 'ITWN' in s: return 'ITWN'
    if 'CSKR' in s: return 'CSKR'
    if 'CNYA' in s: return 'CNYA'
    if sec == 'CASH' or 'CASH' in s: return 'Cash'
    if sec == 'CFD': return 'US Tech CFDs'
    if sec == 'STK' and not any(x in s for x in ['IB01','CSPX','CNDX','SGLN','IGLN','ITWN','CSKR','CNYA']):
        # Dynamically checks the native currency from the DB schema
        return 'Physical US Stocks' if curr == 'USD' else 'International Stocks'
    if sec == 'OPT':
        if pos > 0: 
            try:
                parts = s.split('_')
                if len(parts) >= 4:
                    right = parts[3]
                    exp_date = pd.to_datetime(parts[1])
                    dte = (exp_date - pd.Timestamp.today()).days
                    
                    # PATCH: Classify VIX Calls as Black Swan Tail Hedges
                    if parts[0] == 'VIX' and right == 'C':
                        return 'Tail Hedge'
                        
                    if right == 'P' and dte > 60:
                        # Broad Market Whitelist prevents Decapitation Bug for Sector Shorts (like SMH)
                        if parts[0] in ['SPY', 'SPX', 'XSP', 'QQQ', 'NDX', 'XND']:
                            return 'Tail Hedge'
                    elif right == 'C' and dte > 90:
                        return 'Synthetic Beta'
            except: pass
        return 'Opt Liab'
    return 'Active Swing'
    
pos_df['asset_class'] = pos_df.apply(lambda r: categorize(r['symbol'], r['sec_type'], r['position'], r['currency']), axis=1)

    conn.close()    
    return global_df, global_metrics, silo_dfs, silo_metrics, pos_df, attr_df, df, open_orders_df

swan_shock_pct = sim_crash_input / 100.0
swan_vix_spike = 0.80

# 2. Equity & Synthetic Beta Losses (with Alpha Ledger Slippage Penalty)
swan_phys_loss = 0.0
swan_slippage = 0.10 # 10% gap down slippage penalty on stops

if 'df_alpha' in locals() and not df_alpha.empty:
    for _, r in df_alpha.iterrows():
        spot_usd = r['Spot Price']
        shock_price = spot_usd * (1 - swan_shock_pct)
        for chunk in r['stop_details']:
            q = chunk['q']
            sl_usd = chunk['sl_usd']
            if sl_usd > 0 and shock_price < sl_usd:
                # Stop triggered. Assume 10% slippage, but capped at the gap price
                fill_price = min(sl_usd * (1 - swan_slippage), spot_usd)
                fill_price = max(fill_price, shock_price)
                chunk_loss = (spot_usd - fill_price) * q
            else:
                # Unprotected or SL so low it wasn't triggered
                chunk_loss = (spot_usd - shock_price) * q
            swan_phys_loss += chunk_loss
